entries.title: No-Stakes Baseball Doesn’t Exist — Not Even at Nats Park
entries.summary: The Nationals’ season is going off the rails, but that doesn’t mean the games don’t matter.
entries.content:
On Monday night at Nationals Park, it was possible to have an entire section to yourself, which was how I wound up sitting with a man named Aman Kedir. Sometime in the middle innings, wondering who exactly was taking in a late-August game between the Nationals and Rockies, I spotted Kedir, all alone in Section 226, from the press box. On my way to him, the upper-deck concourse was so quiet I could hear the pitcher grunting on the mound. With no lines for beer, it took a drunk dude about 15 seconds to go from cursing about a lost bet to buying a cold Bud Light. Two 20-somethings leaned on a railing that overlooked the Potomac River, their tall boys sweating onto the concrete floor. The moon cast a rippling spotlight on the water.

They didn’t care who was winning. They might have been falling in love.

It was the kind of dissonance that’s become a constant in D.C., a perfect night for a baseball game that could do nothing to affect the playoff race. Kedir, it turned out, didn’t care who was winning, either. He did, however, care a lot about being there at all, seeing that he had now been to every Major League Baseball stadium. Nationals Park was his last to cross off.

From Row 1, Seat 13 in 226, he told me about knocking out his last four this month, when he realized he had airline miles to burn. His rooting interests? Nice weather, good food, maybe a steal for Nationals outfielder Jacob Young, who is on Kedir’s fantasy team. Then as we chatted, Young came to the plate, which made me say: “Hey! Here he is! Aman, let’s get a steal for you.”

There are, of course, strict rules against cheering of any sort in the press box. But I was in Section 226, which was empty aside from Kedir until it was empty aside from Kedir and me. Young singled and we high-fived. Under my breath, while Kedir kept recapping his ballpark tour, I whispered: “Steal, steal, steal.” The universe, though, didn’t hear me. Jorbit Vivas singled behind Young, moving him to second base. Then the next batter, Nasim Nuñez, dropped down a bunt, which led to Young scoring on a Rockies error.

“OK, OK! There it is!” Kedir, who lives in Minneapolis, said while Young crossed the plate. “I’ll take a run!”

Why he was there was no longer a mystery to me. As for everyone else, I didn’t get to poll the entire stadium, though it would have made for an interesting exit survey. That game, an eventual 13-3 win for the Nats, was between two losing teams near the end of another lost season in D.C. Before the trade deadline, at which the Nationals traded three of their best players, they were 55-58, hanging off the edge of the wild-card race (though hanging nonetheless). But in the three weeks since, they are 8-15, including a 1-8 record on their most recent road trip.

They would also lose to the Rockies (52-82), 13-1, on Wednesday night, which ended with first-year Manager Blake Butera slamming his team’s effort. Even after a 7-1 win Thursday, the Nationals could very well finish last in the National League East, should they slip behind the Mets in the final five weeks of the season. Hope can flip to nihilism in a hurry. Just ask the biggest Nats fan in your life.

And yet, having spent the last few days at the park, I couldn’t shake the idea that baseball with no stakes is an overplayed myth this time of year. Yes, it’s been too long since the Lerner family ran the Nationals with a competitive payroll, which is the only change that could really shift the vibes around here, no matter how savvy the new front office and coaching staff might be. For the necessary amount of cynicism given the recent results, read that sentence again. But beyond the obvious reasons for the players to keep showing up, baseball is still entertainment, community, a way to have a conversation with a stranger that winds from favorite ballparks to minimalist art. And beyond hanging with Kedir, there were other reasons this week to believe in the dull practice of playing out the string, standings and scoreboard be damned.

There was pitcher Matt Waldron, who made his Nationals debut Wednesday after two teams released him in the last month. He is, at 29, looking for a baseball home, pitching for the chance to keep pitching in D.C. or elsewhere. He started Wednesday, allowing two hits and no runs in two innings. Waldron also throws a knuckleball in an era in which the fun-house pitch is almost extinct.

And then there was Luis Perales, a rookie pitcher who made his major league debut in the fifth Wednesday. That was going well until the seventh, when he gave up a two-out grand slam. But when he FaceTimed his mother Tuesday, her tears had nothing to do with whether his first appearance would be perfect. She cried because he’d made it. It was a moment they’ll never forget.

When, on Monday, the press box announced a paid attendance of 12,105, a fan in the 300 level screamed: “Liars!” He got some laughs. But even on slow nights, a stadium is like an airport or a shopping mall, a whole city unto itself. I saw grade-school siblings sharing a lemonade, the brother’s arm around his sister’s shoulders. I watched two stadium employees high-five in an empty team store, laughing their heads off. I briefly adopted a fantasy squad.

For at least a little while, I stopped wondering why anyone cared.

Before the series began, Butera fielded a handful of questions about how to keep his players and staff motivated. This is new territory for Butera in two ways: He has never managed into a quiet September of a major-league season. And, until a few weeks ago, he had never managed a team that wasn’t pushing for a long-shot playoff spot.

The answers, though, didn’t require experience in the chair. This is the big leagues. The process is important, as are the results for a group of young, unproven players trying to earn future opportunities. For him, for the next month and change, what matters is that the Nationals play hard, even if they sometimes play at a much lower level than their contending opponents.

He was certainly not satisfied Wednesday. Then Thursday was much better, another data point for a team that’s figuring out what it has moving forward — and on the flip side, what it needs.

There is, then, a big difference between baseball with no playoff implications and baseball that means nothing at all. The former happened at Nationals Park this week. I’m fairly certain the latter does not exist. In the seventh inning Monday, I was typing up some notes, head buried in my laptop, when Jay Z’s “Young Forever” blared over the speakers. That could only mean Jacob Young was up again, so I lowered my screen to lock in. He laced a double to left-center, missing a homer by a few feet. Excited, I whipped my head to 226, hoping to catch Kedir’s reaction.

But what I found this time was a completely empty section. My new friend had exercised one of the golden freedoms of a game with few fans. He had moved for another view.
entries.author: Jesse Dougherty

entries.title: Gas Prices Are High. Trump’s Supporters Are Feeling The Most Pain.
entries.summary: We crunched the numbers: Pain at the pump is sharper on one side of the political spectrum.
entries.content:
Gas at the pump costs 40% more than it did before the Iran war began in February, according to the Energy Information Administration. And whether you’re a die-hard Democrat or red-blooded Republican or somewhere in between, everyone pays directly or indirectly for that hike.

Historically, this would be awful news for the White House occupant. Political scientists seem to agree that, unlike some trends that preoccupy pundits, gas prices really do move the needle on presidential approval.

Gasoline is a substantial part of the typical family’s budget, of course, but its real influence may lie in its simplicity. As Northwestern University’s Laurel Harbridge-Yong said on Matt Grossmann’s “The Science of Politics” podcast, you drive by gas stations with enormous price signs all the time. If you have a gas-powered car, you fill up regularly, so you have a common point of comparison. And, unlike with groceries where the long receipt obfuscates individual changes, you watch your wallet empty as your car fills up.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/B8v0g/3/

In a 2016 book chapter, an all-star team of Harbridge-Yong and co-authors Jon Krosnick of Stanford University and Jeffrey Wooldridge of Michigan State University assembled three decades of presidential approval ratings, compared them to gas-price data, and found that every 10-cent rise in gas prices led to as much as a 0.6 percentage-point drop in the president’s approval rating. That held true even after controlling for food-and-beverage inflation, unemployment and presidential scandals. Simply put, voter sentiment often follows the gas gauge.

In the years since, other scholars have found similar trends. American Politics Research analysis shows that people living in places with longer car commutes are more likely to punish the president’s party for rising gas prices.

In an apparent effort to blunt this poll penalty in the upcoming midterms, President Donald Trump has often tried to justify the higher prices.

“So I just say this, so for you to pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline,” he told the crowd at an event this month on Long Island, “just remember, you're doing it so that a very evil country cannot have … a nuclear weapon. So remember that, when you have to pay a little bit more.”

And support for the president does seem to cloud our views on the price surge. A recent YouGov poll found 32% of Republicans said gas prices were going up a lot, compared with 60% of Democrats.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/GkJpk/1/



In reality, since the war began in February, pump prices have leapt more than a dollar in both the reddest and bluest counties, with little variation based on politics, according to data from AAA and OPIS, the oil-price geniuses at Dow Jones. (The exception is Indiana, which now has the lowest gas prices in the nation after Republican Gov. Mike Braun suspended the state’s gas tax of about 60 cents a gallon.)

But, as our colleague Thomas Burr pointed out, it’s not just the change in price that determines how much gas prices hit your wallet. It’s how much you drive.

Seen through that lens, the initial results look pretty simple: The pain falls more heavily on Trump’s base. About 87% of workers in the Trumpiest fifth of the country commute by car, according to our analysis of the American Community Survey. That’s almost 40% more than the fifth of the country that went most heavily for Kamala Harris in 2024.



We can blame much of the gap on the urban-rural divide. Rural regions that went for Harris tend to drive a fair bit as well, but they’re rarer than rural red counties.

But gas prices can vary by well over a dollar per gallon depending on where you live, so isn’t it possible that, while Democrats tend to live in areas where people drive less, they also pay more per gallon?

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7MCoZ/1/



Yes! We estimate Americans living in the bluest fifth of the country pay almost 20% more per gallon, extrapolating from data from AAA.



So, that raises the ultimate question: Does the higher price in Democratic-leaning counties offset the fact that they tend to drive less?

It’s tricky to account for the actual miles driven in each county. The best source might be 2017 data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics, which — while stale — tends to agree with more recent (albeit spottier) data from other sources.

If we use that data to account for the miles driven by households in each county, combined with spending data from the Energy Information Administration, we find that households in the reddest fifth of America still spend about 30% more on gasoline in a typical year than their friends in the bluest areas.

And if you look at it as a share of income — to account for the fact that city jobs tend to pay more — households in the reddest areas shell out about twice as much of their paychecks as their bluest buddies.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/TJq58/1/



That may be part of why even Republicans seem to be souring on the Trump economy.

“Republicans saw a pretty big decrease in sentiment this month,” said Joanne Hsu, director of the widely watched University of Michigan Survey of Consumers. “It’s the lowest we’ve seen since the start of this administration.”

When respondents are asked to explain their answers, she said, everybody is far more likely to point to gas prices these days, but Republicans remain a bit less likely to cite them specifically. It’s an echo of the YouGov poll above — Republicans don’t see gas prices rising as fast, even though they’re hit hardest at the pump.

But is it just partisan wishful thinking?

Hsu had another explanation. Later in their survey, they ask where folks expect gas prices to go in the next year. Democrats and independents both thought they’d keep on climbing, while Republicans were the only group that expected gas to get cheaper.

https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Ivjnd/4/



“Republicans are still giving the president a little latitude on that,” Hsu said, “because there’s a belief that as soon as the war is over, gas prices are going to come down.”

“If you think it’s just a short-term pinch, you might have a higher tolerance for it,” she added. “You can stomach it because you don’t think it’s going to last.”
entries.author: Andrew Van Dam

entries.title: Trump’s Quietly Working to Give Part of Yosemite to a Private Developer
entries.summary: The National Park Service is under pressure to make an unprecedented deal that cedes a quarter-mile strip of the park.
entries.content:
For more than a year, the National Park Service has been quietly working to fulfill an unprecedented directive from Trump officials: Parcel off a corner of Yosemite National Park to give to a private developer.

National Park Service staff in California and Washington, D.C., are trying to arrange a land exchange between a Nevada-based company and the federal government, according to four people directly familiar with discussions, as well as agency documents reviewed by NOTUS.

Since the spring of 2025, the Trump administration has been looking into ways it could cede a roughly quarter-mile strip of land inside Yosemite to a company that, through a web of limited-liability companies, is operated by real-estate developer and investment firm Kingsbarn Realty Capital. Officials are proposing the Park Service give up the land or “interest” in the land in the form of an easement, and in return receive land of equal value somewhere in California that has yet to be decided.

The private developers own an 83-acre plot of land just outside the western boundaries of Yosemite, about five miles from one of the park’s defining ancient sequoia groves. Jeff Pori, the CEO of Kingsbarn, wants to build a short road connecting the property to one of Yosemite’s central thoroughfares. The new road would give the land exceptionally rare private access to a park that is otherwise almost entirely buffered by national forests.

The property’s current access road is more than 10 miles from an entrance to the park, and much further from Yosemite’s most iconic sights. Without a new road, visitors to the property — whether it be developed into a hotel, resort or private residence — would need to drive an hour and a half in a circuitous route to reach the popular Yosemite Valley.

The planning process has created a tense environment inside the National Park Service for the people involved; Kingsbarn’s proposal is backed by the full weight of the Interior Department’s top political leadership, sources said.

“They want us to be responsive to the property owner and their lobbyists or people, and they want us to work with these folks,” said one person familiar with the conversations.

“The political pressure being brought to bear is very unusual,” said another person familiar with the conversations and the park’s history.

If the deal goes through, the Trump administration would be breaking with 150 years of American precedent at the birthplace of the national park system. The federal government has historically strived to expand the crown-jewel national parks, not give up land within them.

“The national park idea started in Yosemite with Abraham Lincoln’s preservation of Yosemite Valley and the Mariposa Grove of giant sequoias,” said Cicely Muldoon, a 40-year veteran of the Park Service who served as Yosemite’s superintendent for about five years. Muldoon retired from Yosemite shortly after President Donald Trump took office in 2025.
Yosemite Climate Change (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)“Our basic purpose in the national parks is to preserve these places unimpaired for future generations, not letting go of that for the purpose of private profit,” she said.

Interior’s advocacy for the deal is a significant reversal of a pledge Secretary Doug Burgum made in his 2025 confirmation hearing: “The national parks, absolutely we need to support and protect every single inch of those,” he said.

It also contravenes the presidential message Trump shared on Aug. 24 of this year, to announce the beginning of National Park Week: “My Administration is committed to protecting every acre of our lands and preserving the cleanest air and water in the world."

And it goes against the agency’s past position on this specific piece of land. The Park Service has received this privatization request before, and it has rejected it repeatedly for over two decades.

In a statement to NOTUS, a spokesperson for the National Park Service said “no final decisions have been made,” but that any land exchange or access proposals “would be subject to all applicable federal laws, regulations, and Departmental policies, including required environmental review and public notification processes.”

“If a proposal advances, the Department would follow established procedures to ensure appropriate coordination, transparency, and public involvement, consistent with federal law,” the spokesperson said.

Kingsbarn did not respond to a request for comment.

A limited-liability company controlled by Kingsbarn purchased the undeveloped land outside Yosemite for $4 million in 2024, calling the property “Sanctuary at Yosemite” in records reviewed by NOTUS.
https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/42sjZ/1/Historically the land was called Hazel Green Ranch. Its previous owner was a California developer named Lewis Geyser, who had tried for years to persuade the Bush administration, and then the Obama administration, to let him build a short private road in Yosemite. He planned to develop Hazel Green Ranch as a resort.

In the early 2000s, the Park Service appeared interested in the possibility of working with Geyser as part of a broader plan to dramatically reduce the development pressure on the Yosemite Valley. But that plan quickly collapsed, and the National Park Service in turn refused to allow any further development within the boundaries of Yosemite.

Geyser eventually sued in 2007 to try to force the issue, losing first in district court and again on appeal in 2012.

Both times, the judges ruled that Geyser did not have a claim to a private road. While the federal government has an obligation to provide an exit for private properties completely enclosed by federal lands, it doesn’t have to allow for new roads when one already exists. The land’s existing access road — albeit old, long and winding — runs through Forest Service lands.

When Kingsbarn took over the land from Geyser in 2024, Pori’s company almost immediately approached Interior about again trying to build the private road.

“We got an email from the new owner, reopening this issue that we felt was long closed,” Muldoon said. “Whoever bought the land hadn't done their due diligence and realized that this was not a possibility by law, to build a new entrance essentially into Yosemite National Park for private purposes. So happily, when I left, it was still in that place.”

But whereas the Bush, Obama and Biden administrations said no, Trump’s Interior is pushing hard to say yes.
FL22212.jpg (4902x3672, AR: 1.33)Every few weeks, at the direction of their political superiors, staff at the Park Service have scheduled meetings with Kingsbarn, multiple sources said. Pori sometimes attends the meetings with his associates, including Lanny Davis, a lobbyist who served as an adviser to Bill and Hillary Clinton and represented a list of controversial clients including Michael Cohen, Harvey Weinstein and the former dictator of Equatorial Guinea. Davis has not listed Kingsbarn or Pori as clients in his federal lobbying disclosures.

Staff are required to send regular updates on their progress to political appointees inside Burgum’s office, and they are occasionally berated by political staff for not moving fast enough, according to two people familiar with the process.

The current superintendent of Yosemite, Ray McPadden, has been pressured by people at the Interior Department and has tried to help move the land exchange along, according to two people familiar with his role.

Under the rules that govern public lands, any land that the Park Service chooses to surrender must be replaced by land of equivalent value.

While land exchanges are quite common for the federal government, they usually begin with an agency identifying a piece of land it wants to add to a park or forest. The Park Service trying to give a piece of a park to a private individual is an “unusual case,” said one former Park Service official, who added that the pursuit of this deal in secret makes it especially unprecedented.

For the exchange to happen, NPS has to appraise the land inside the park and identify land it wants somewhere else in California of equivalent value. The developer would then need to acquire the property and give it to the Park Service in the exchange.

The appraisal of the land within Yosemite is currently ongoing and is a difficult and lengthy task, sources said. How to value a piece of Yosemite is a hard question to answer — and likely cannot account for how the land is eventually developed, however lucrative that may be.

“Obviously this looks kind of unseemly, with the value of this property potentially exploding with the deal,” said one person familiar with the agency’s conversations. “They may give them acreage somewhere else to add to a national park unit that is ostensibly of equal value, but to the developer the value of the ultimate Hazel Green deal is incredible.”

“It kind of smells, you know. It’s not quite right,” they added.

Pori has had public business ties to people in Trump’s orbit.

In April 2025, Kingsbarn Realty Capital closed a deal to acquire the Los Angeles headquarters of Kim Kardashian’s lingerie company Skims, working with two companies with links to the Trump administration: the Newmark Group and Hankey Capital. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick chaired the Newmark Group before entering the Trump administration, and did not fully divest from the company until May 2025. Don Hankey, the chair of Hankey Capital, is also the chair of an insurance company that underwrote Trump’s $175 million bond in his appeal in 2024 of a New York civil fraud judgment.

Pori personally thanked both companies in the press release announcing the deal, which he said was made possible in part by Hankey Capital.

Between 2024 and 2025, Pori made monthly, largely small-dollar donations to the Republican Party committee, Trump’s campaign committee and associated PACs. Pori does not have a history of donating to national political campaign efforts before October 2024, according to a NOTUS analysis of the Federal Election Commission donor database.

Neither Pori nor the Interior Department have publicly expressed interest in the Yosemite land exchange.
America 250 Trump Roosevelt Library (8355x5570, AR: 1.50)Early this year, members of Congress were notified for the first time that the Park Service was considering the land exchange in Yosemite. The notification was vague. It implied that the Land and Water Conservation Fund would be used to enable the exchange but gave no details about the valuation of the land in Yosemite or what the Park Service might accept in return. It did not name the developer or indicate that the exchange was a high priority.

Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), the chair and ranking member of the Senate Appropriations subcommittee with oversight of the Land and Water Conservation Fund, sent Interior a list of projects that they endorse for the fund; the proposal for Yosemite was not on the list.

“The Senate Interior-Environment Appropriations Subcommittee Chair and Ranking Member told the Interior Department which projects they agreed on to go forward. That didn’t include the Yosemite project, which Senator Merkley objected to,” said Justin Krakoff, the deputy communications director for Merkley.

Murkowski’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

California’s two Democratic senators told NOTUS they opposed the proposed exchange.

“The Land and Water Conservation Fund exists to acquire land and interests in land in order to safeguard natural areas, water resources, and cultural heritage — and to provide recreation opportunities for all Americans,” Sen. Alex Padilla said. “Projects should be chosen on merit, not on an applicant's connections to high-ranking Trump Administration officials.”

“Yosemite is one of California’s natural wonders and must be protected from further development. The courts struck this project down once, but this administration appears hellbent on moving forward in the face of opposition from the public, Congress and the courts. But the only thing the administration cares about is whether there is money involved. We will fight this again,” said Sen. Adam Schiff.

The Park Service can likely move forward on a land exchange without any further congressional involvement.

If the land exchange eventually occurs as planned, it is likely that it will face a legal challenge from environmental and conservation groups.

The National Parks Conservation Association said it strongly opposes the plan.

“After a century of protecting Yosemite, the National Park Service is now working in overdrive to turn over land to a private developer in a secretive, backroom deal. This is an attack on the American people that own this national park. It would also be unlawful and a court previously rejected a road development proposal,” said Mark Rose, the group’s Sierra Nevada program manager.

He would not comment on the group’s legal strategy.
entries.author: Anna Kramer

entries.title: DCA Has Trouble (Again) Reaching the President’s Helicopter
entries.summary: Air traffic controllers had to communicate with Marine One via other aircraft hours after an investigation into an Aug. 4 communications breakdown was released.
entries.content:
The president’s helicopter experienced an apparent loss of communication with Ronald Reagan National Airport on Thursday, as President Donald Trump was leaving the White House for a trip to Texas. The issue occurred hours after an investigation found that Marine One experienced issues communicating with the same airport during a separate incident earlier this month.

Before lifting off from the Ellipse, air traffic controllers at DCA had an exchange with another helicopter about Marine One’s failure to communicate with the tower.

“Eagle Two, Marine One is trying to reach you at three minutes to lift,” a pilot told the tower, identifying his aircraft and conveying the president’s impending departure.

“Oh, I couldn’t hear any of that,” an air traffic controller responded.

Once alerted, the tower asked the pilot when Marine One had communicated with him, saying they were trying to coordinate. The tower again reached out to Marine One, which didn’t respond. The air traffic controller radioed another helicopter that was a member of the presidential Marine One squadron.

“Nighthawk Eight, do me a favor, I can’t hear Marine One,” a controller said. “If you hear Marine One, can you let me know?”

The tower reconnected with Marine One after about 43 seconds.

The disconnect happened after a preliminary investigation found that air traffic controllers at Reagan warned about having communications issues with the Marine Corps helicopter squadron staff before an aircraft flew within a mile of the president’s helicopter earlier this month.

A domestic passenger jet and Marine One came within 0.82 lateral miles of each other with Trump on board, after Marine One tried to reach the tower twice but didn’t get through. The incident — what the Federal Aviation Administration calls a “loss of standard separation” — occurred a week after a meeting to devise alternative communication methods in case of such issues.

When asked about Thursday’s radio failure, an FAA spokesperson told NOTUS in a statement that the agency took immediate action after the Aug. 4 incident, including relocating an antenna to improve communications between DCA air traffic controllers and Marine One pilots.

“The three-minute notification was communicated by alternate means, acknowledged by a controller and positive contact was established with Marine One before takeoff,” the FAA spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority directed NOTUS to the FAA.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Marine One lifted off from the Ellipse at 3:03 p.m. on Thursday, ferrying Trump to Joint Base Andrews. After the Aug. 4 incident, FAA technicians found that there was “not adequate line-of-sight to ensure communications between the radio transmitter/receiver and The Ellipse.”

Marine One has been departing from the Ellipse while construction on a helipad on the White House South Lawn is ongoing. Trump said last week that he anticipates construction to be completed in late September.
entries.author: Ben T.N. Mause

entries.title: Judge Says Pentagon Illegally Blacklisted Anthropic
entries.summary: “The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin wrote.
entries.content:
A federal judge struck down the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic, ruling Thursday that the Trump administration illegally retaliated against the artificial intelligence company for criticizing the government.

U.S. District Judge Rita F. Lin found that the administration violated Anthropic’s First Amendment and due process rights and that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth improperly designated the company a national-security supply chain risk.

“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” Lin wrote.

The ruling vacated Hegseth’s designation and barred the administration from enforcing the measures Anthropic challenged.

Anthropic sued after the Pentagon designated it a supply chain risk and moved to cut it off from federal work. The company argued that officials retaliated after it resisted demands to remove restrictions on using its Claude models for mass domestic surveillance of Americans and fully autonomous weapons.

The ruling confirms concerns Lin raised at a hearing last month, when she said the government had failed to produce evidence showing Anthropic posed the threat officials claimed.

Lin found that Anthropic’s public criticism was a substantial factor in the government’s actions. She pointed to statements from President Donald Trump and Hegseth attacking the company and said officials sought to “make a public example out of Anthropic” after the dispute became public.

The administration argued that Anthropic could not be trusted and that its conduct raised concerns it could interfere with military systems.

Lin rejected that argument, saying she found no “articulable basis” to believe Anthropic would sabotage its models and said the government had not shown the company could alter them after they were deployed on national security systems.

“An IT vendor does not become a potential adversary of the United States whenever it asks probing questions or stubbornly insists on particular contracting terms, even if doing so causes DoW to doubt its trustworthiness,” Lin wrote.

Anthropic praised the ruling.

“We welcome the court’s ruling that this supply chain risk designation was unlawful. We remain focused on working productively with the government to harness AI for our national security so all Americans benefit from this technology,” an Anthropic spokesperson told The Verge.

The Pentagon did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Anthropic was the first U.S. company publicly designated a supply chain risk under the law the Pentagon invoked, which is intended to protect military systems from threats including sabotage. Lin found that Anthropic’s contract dispute and public criticism did not meet the law’s definition of a supply chain risk.

The judge also found that the administration’s continued dealings with Anthropic also undermined its national security argument.

A day after Anthropic was formally designated a supply chain risk, Pentagon under secretary Emil Michael told the company that the two sides were “very close” to reaching a deal. The White House later discussed possible uses of Anthropic’s newer Mythos model in sensitive settings, according to the ruling.

“None of that is consistent with a genuine fear that Anthropic is a saboteur who would poison its software to harm national security,” Lin wrote.

Lin also found problems with how the Pentagon reached its decision.

Hegseth publicly ordered the designation before officials completed the analysis supporting it. The Pentagon prepared the factual basis afterward, which Lin said suggested the record was assembled “after the fact to justify the foreordained conclusion.”

The Pentagon also failed to adequately consider less-restrictive alternatives and did not give congressional committees the explanation required under federal law. Lin found the designation was “arbitrary and capricious.”

The ruling does not require the Pentagon to use Anthropic’s technology. The Pentagon had continued removing Anthropic’s technology from military systems while the case was pending and expected to finish that process by the end of September, government lawyers said at last month’s hearing.

The government is expected to challenge Thursday’s ruling.

Anthropic has a separate case pending in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit challenging a related supply chain risk designation issued under a different federal law.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Trump’s Mail-In Ballots Plan Blocked by Judge Yet Again
entries.summary: The federal judge’s ruling came hours after the U.S. Postal Service said Trump’s order was in effect.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Thursday again blocked President Donald Trump’s crackdown on mail-in ballots, in an order that came down shortly after the U.S. Postal Service said the new requirements were in effect following a protracted legal battle.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani’s ruling is likely to be appealed by the Trump administration, further delaying implementation of an executive order that, if allowed to move forward, would have profound implications for this year’s midterm elections. Under Trump’s order, the Postal Service would compare ballots sent through the mail to a list of eligible voters created by the federal government.

In her ruling Thursday, Talwani said plaintiff states faced a prohibitively short timeline to follow through with the rule’s demands and blocked it for at least 14 days. The next hearing in the case is scheduled for Sept. 3.

“Plaintiff States have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal, and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms,” Talwani wrote.

Trump signed an executive order in March that sought to redefine the federal government’s role in the election process. Nearly two dozen states and the District of Columbia swiftly sued, arguing the order was a violation of their constitutional rights to administer elections.

Talwani, an Obama appointee, blocked parts of Trump’s order in two separate cases filed in Boston earlier this summer. But the Supreme Court halted Talwani’s injunction on Monday, finding that she had acted too soon because federal agencies had not yet implemented the executive order. 

The Supreme Court’s order did not decide whether Trump’s policy mandates were lawful, but it did provide a temporary win for the president’s administration.

The Postal Service acknowledged Thursday there was “pending litigation” on the final rule and would continue to provide updates “as necessary.”

entries.title: What the Flock?
entries.content:
Good morning. This is the NOTUS Metro newsletter for Aug. 28, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

THE LATEST

Flock has its eyes on D.C., but we know surprisingly little about how the powerful license plate readers are used.

The cameras have drawn plenty of national attention recently, with reports of police officers using them and the data they store to track their former lovers and commit other abuses. Civil liberties groups have also raised concerns of mass surveillance of otherwise law-abiding motorists.

But proponents hail Flock as a powerful tool to fight crime, especially because — unlike past iterations of license plate readers — it allows police in one jurisdiction to search the databases for license plates scanned in others. Police officials say this allows for almost real-time tracking of vehicles and suspects — including as they cross county or state lines.

D.C. has 67 Flock cameras, capable of scanning some 400,000 license plates every day — data that is then kept for 90 days. Police officials say the cameras have helped solve crimes, including at least two homicides last year. The footage also gives the Metropolitan Police Department the ability to track suspects if they flee the city.

Little else is known about how the massive amount of data has been used. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle and Jenny Gathright report that MPD set up some guardrails for its system this year, but it went almost a full year with no such limits in place. Additionally, MPD has rejected open-records requests — including one from NOTUS — for data on who has been searching the city’s database, and why.

D.C. lawmakers have largely been quiet on Flock, though At-Large council member Christina Henderson has sought answers from MPD. She says that her views on the technology have evolved over the past few months, and that she thinks MPD is using it appropriately. Still, she understands why some residents may have concerns.

“I think we have to figure out what the balance is, and I think that’s the conversation that we should be having as policymakers,” she says. “Not necessarily to completely discard a system, but to ensure there are protocols and guardrails in place, and also periodic audits to make sure that those who have been ensured with this system are using it appropriately.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

A special grand jury empaneled by U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro has been looking into truancy and graduation rates in D.C. Public Schools, The Washington Post reports. The rarely used tool allows prosecutors to investigate but not necessarily file charges for wrongdoing — the grand jury can instead issue a report on its investigation.

Pirro has raised concerns about oversight of D.C. teenagers over the past year, threatening to prosecute parents for allowing their children out past curfew and pushing to change city law to give her office authority to prosecute more teens as adults.

What will D.C. do with its Meta millions? Henderson suggested Thursday on X that the District could “finally” fund a youth psychiatric treatment facility in the city with the settlement money from the social media giant.

The tribe has spoken. A federal prosecutor living in D.C. is among the castaways set to compete on the 51st season of “Survivor,” People magazine reports.

Hyperlocal politics can get physical, it seems. An advisory neighborhood commissioner in Ward 5 has been charged with simple assault after authorities said she shoved a woman at a public meeting. The dispute stemmed from a disagreement over a proposed bike lane in the Bloomingdale neighborhood. Karla Lewis, the accused commissioner, has raised concerns over the bike lane that could run along R Street Northwest.





FROM MARYLAND

The University of Maryland’s flagship campus in College Park is predicting a 30% decline in new graduate student enrollment this fall due to President Donald Trump’s new visa restrictions, The Banner reports.



METRO MOMENTS

Natty Nationals dog extra (1938x1280, AR: 1.51)
Last month, we sent photographer Jared Soares out to Nats Park to take some pictures of Natty, the much-loved team dog. Our story on Natty came out earlier this week, and we would highly recommend checking it out. But there were just too many good photos to choose from. So, here’s a favorite from the cutting room floor. 





SPORTS

The Nats are no longer in the playoff hunt, but that doesn’t mean this season has lost all meaning. In fact, NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty argues that the idea of no-stakes baseball is a myth. Every game means a whole lot to somebody, whether it’s a captivated fan in Section 226 or a recent call-up on the mound.

Fire away, Commanders fans: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson will be doing an AMA at noon today over on r/Commanders.

What to Watch This Weekend

Friday

NFL preseason: Commanders at Ravens, 6 p.m. (WUSA9)

MLB: Nationals vs. Marlins, 6:45 p.m. (Fox5)

WNBA: Mystics at Sparks, 10 p.m. (Ion)

Saturday

Sunday

entries.title: Uneven Pain at the Pump
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Gas hikes are felt more by one side of the political spectrum. A Democratic candidate snags another Republican staffer. A developer has a good shot at getting a slice of Yosemite. And: Governors’ races could make or break a Democratic majority.





THE LATEST

The results are in: Donald Trump’s supporters are shouldering more of the pain at the pump, even if they’re not complaining about it as much. Gas prices are up, on average, more than a buck since the Iran war began, and Americans are ponying up more to fill the tank — but they’re not suffering equally.

NOTUS’ resident data guru, Andrew Van Dam, dug into the numbers: About 87% of workers in the Trumpiest fifth of the U.S. commute by car, almost 40% more than the fifth of the country that went most heavily for Kamala Harris in 2024. And even though there are higher prices in Democratic-leaning counties (read: Los Angeles County), it was offset by the fact that they tend to drive less, and that city jobs tend to pay more.

Households in the reddest areas allocate about twice as much of their income as their bluest buddies for gas. Here’s the but: When asked how gas prices will fare in the next 12 months, Republicans are the only ones optimistically saying they’ll drop.

“Republicans are still giving the president a little latitude on that,” said Joanne Hsu, who watches consumers at the University of Michigan, “because there’s a belief that as soon as the war is over, gas prices are going to come down.”

Open tabs: Putin sees U.S. as weakened by Iran war, intelligence reports say (WaPo); Trump Plans to Mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, Not Ground Zero (NYT); Judge again blocks Trump mail ballot executive order (AP); ICE agent arrested for shooting released from Texas jail (Star Tribune); U.S. close to striking “massive” deal for Venezuelan oil fields (Axios)





From the campaign trail


First on NOTUS: Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Adam Hamilton hired a longtime Republican staffer to lead his campaign’s digital operations, NOTUS’ Igor Bobic scoops, joining fellow red-state Senate Democratic candidate James Talarico of Texas in bringing on bipartisan help as a way to appeal to moderate voters in November.

Austin Gilpin, who previously worked for the Republican firm America Rising, Rep. Ron Estes and the Kansas Republican Party, signed up in June as Hamilton’s campaign digital director. Gilpin said in a statement that Republican Sen. Roger Marshall has chosen “his party and his president over Kansas, and over decency,” and that the incumbent “doesn’t speak up when the federal government oversteps.”

“I didn’t leave my values behind when I joined Adam’s campaign,” Gilpin said. “Republicans always have a seat at his table, and he is earning their support the same way he earned mine.”

Coming to a town near you: Protect Our Care is launching a tour this October, driving a bus emblazoned with its message of “Sick of It! Fix Health Care Now” across 14 states with 40 stops, including in Maine, Pennsylvania and Michigan. The left-leaning health-care advocacy group is targeting Republicans’ big legislative achievement, the One Big Beautiful Bill, which made cuts to public health insurance.

Election deniers are on the ballot this year, and if they win, they’ll be uniquely positioned to run the same elections they’ve often called into question, NOTUS’ Adora Brown reports. The candidates aren’t just positioning themselves in deep-red states, but also three key 2028 swing states: Nevada, Arizona and Wisconsin. And while Trump has largely stayed out of races for the top election-official position, they could be some of his most crucial allies as he pushes to obtain voter rolls and federalize election oversight.

“They may just willingly give up election materials. They may just willingly give up cast ballots. They may just willingly give up election machines,” said Edward Caspar, chief counsel for the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law.





THE BIG ONE

Yo, what? The National Park Service is working to give a corner of Yosemite National Park to a private developer as part of a land exchange. NOTUS Anna Kramer reports that the Park Service has been quietly working — under orders from Interior Department top brass — to give an easement for a roughly quarter-mile strip of land inside the park to a Nevada-based company that owns an 85-acre plot just outside Yosemite. The CEO of Kingsbarn Realty Capital, which, through a web of LLCs, operates the ownership of the land, wants to build a road connecting the property to the park, giving the land rare, private access to a shielded part of Yosemite.

People familiar with the conversations told Anna that the unprecedented deal, and the political pressure they are facing to push it through, is a reversal from Interior’s past position on the project.

“It kind of smells, you know,” one person familiar with the plans told Anna, pointing to the potential gain for the private developer. “It’s not quite right.”





NOTUS PERSPECTIVES

Jesse Watters vs. Abdul El-Sayed was not just compelling TV, writes Matt K. Lewis. It was also great for American democracy.





NOTUS METRO

Sign up for our local newsletter, written by Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.

Local news: D.C. Won’t Say How It’s Using Its Flock Cameras, by Martin Austermuhle and Jenny Gathright

Sports desk: No-Stakes Baseball Doesn’t Exist — Not Even at Nats Park, by Jesse Dougherty





NEW ON NOTUS

Keep an eye on the guvs: The House majority could hinge on something completely out of candidates’ control: who wins the governors’ races. With no presidential candidate at the top of the ticket this year, NOTUS’ Paul Kane writes that if Democratic governors maintain their strong polling margins, that could carry down the ballot and help determine who controls the House. In swing states like Arizona and Pennsylvania, winning those governorships could mean a sea change for Democrats.

More: DCA Warned About Communications Issues With Marine One Before August Safety Incident, by Angie Orellana Hernandez

Wyoming Governor Asks State Attorney General to Investigate DOJ Election Observers, by Jenna Monnin

Former Stars and Stripes Journalists Sue Pete Hegseth After Firings, by Torrie Herrington





NOT US

  • Memes and Machine Guns: How Brandon Herrera Built a Path to Congress, by Kiera Butler for Mother Jones
  • NDAs are hiding data center deals, drawing ire from locals — and attention from lawmakers, by Drew Hawkins for NPR
  • What If Canada Joined the E.U.? By Ishaan Tharoor for The New Yorker

entries.title: House Majority Could Hinge on Governors’ Races Trending Toward Democrats
entries.summary: Big wins at top of ticket could propel Democrats down-ballot to a majority.
entries.content:
A pair of polls released early this week reaffirmed the conventional wisdom in two key races: Democratic governors in Arizona and Pennsylvania appear headed for victory.

And the margins in those polls suggested the potential for the type of coattails that could boost Democrats to down-ballot victories and a House majority.

In Arizona, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs held a lead of 15 percentage points over Republican Rep. Andy Biggs, according to an independent firm with roots in Arizona conservative politics. And in Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro had a 16-point lead over the Republican nominee, Stacy Garrity, according to a poll conducted by The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times and Sienna University.

“Gubernatorial races certainly aren’t the be-all, end-all for House contests in their state, but you’d rather be winning those statewide contests than losing them, and Democrats look like they’ll be on the winning side in far more places than Republicans,” Jacob Rubashkin, deputy editor of Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, told NOTUS.

In Arizona and Pennsylvania, Republicans are defending five toss-up seats in the House,with one more in each state that are considered vulnerable.

Those seven seats include six Republican incumbents who have won in tough political environments before, having received crossover votes from people who supported Democrats higher up on the ballot.

But those types of margins for Hobbs and Shapiro, if they hold true in November, will make it an even tougher uphill climb for these Republicans.

In Pennsylvania, like most of the swing states he won two years ago, President Donald Trump is now deeply unpopular, with the new poll finding just 38 percent of voters approved of his job performance. 

Nationally, Democrats stand a chance to claim a majority of the 50 governor’s mansions for the first time since before the 2010 midterm elections.

Republicans currently hold 26, while Democrats hold 24. Of the 36 gubernatorial races this year, Democrats are clearly favored to win 13 and Republicans should easily win 10, according to The Cook Report with Amy Walter’s analysis.

Of the four pure toss-up races, three are currently held by Republicans. Winning a majority would mark a dramatic sea change for Democrats, who after the 2016 elections held just 16 governorships.

The national media spotlight usually shines much brighter on Senate races, but back in the states, gubernatorial battles can often be a bigger driving force in this era of increasing polarization, where fewer voters split their tickets.

And in states like Arizona and Pennsylvania, where there is no Senate race, the battle for top state executive will be the only major statewide race driving turnout this fall.

Republicans believe they gain some potential help from other governors’ races, particularly in Florida. Democrats are defending three competitive House seats and they haven’t won a gubernatorial race there in more than 30 years. Rep. Byron Donalds won the Republican nomination earlier this month, when almost 450,000 more people voted in the GOP primary than in the Democratic primary.

The Arizona poll also might be an outlier as most analysts still believe the race is competitive, with Hobbs having a small but important edge.

While few strategists give Republican Bruce Blakeman a chance to defeat New York Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, his background as a county executive on Long Island has some believing he can boost House Republican challengers there against Democratic Reps. Tom Suozzi and Laura Gillen.

But the broader climate, at this moment, is lifting Democratic spirits, providing openings in some races that might now seem like a reach if the nominees to run the state win big.

In Iowa, state Auditor Rob Sand is now a narrow favorite to become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in 20 years.

“Sand’s strong, well-funded candidacy is contributing to Republicans’ headaches in the state. And it could help deliver multiple House districts to Democrats in November,” Nathan Gonzales wrote last month.

Four years ago, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who is retiring, won reelection by almost 19 points, helping Republicans sweep all four of the state’s House seats for the first time since 1994.

In 2024, even with Trump winning the state by more than 13 points, Iowa Republican Rep. Zach Nunn won by less than 4 percentage points and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks won by about 800 votes.

In 2018, when Reynolds narrowly won the governor’s race, Democrats took three of the delegation’s House seats. Republicans privately hope that since Iowa has an unusual ballot with the governor’s race at the bottom, independent voters will consider those House races separately before viewing the governor’s contest.

Colorado’s transformation from a swing state to reliably blue for Democrats has not — yet — reshaped its House delegation, which is evenly split 4-4 on party lines.

Given Gov. Jared Polis’ 20-point victory four years ago there, Democrats are hoping for another double-digit margin for state Attorney General Phil Weiser in the governor’s race. That would put Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in grave danger in a genuine toss-up race — and it has prompted two previously safe Republicans, Reps. Jeff Crank and Jeff Hurd, to run much harder this cycle than in their previous races.

The Republican nominees for both governor and senator in Colorado have shown little signs of political life, leaving down-ballot Republicans to essentially fend for themselves.

“It’s helpful to have at least one statewide candidate who is adding onto the TV advertising, ground game, and enthusiasm. That’s especially true in a year where Republicans may struggle to turn out the Trump coalition without the president on the ballot,” Inside Elections’ Rubashkin said.

One wild card is California, where three House seats — two Republican, one Democratic — are hotly contested and the governor’s race is all but assured to go to Democrat Xavier Becerra, the former Cabinet secretary and state attorney general.

Republican Rep. David Valadao survived in 2022 despite Gov. Gavin Newsom’s 18-point win statewide, because the Republican gubernatorial nominee narrowly won his Central Valley district.

Valadao probably needs this year’s Republican nominee, political commentator Steve Hilton, to perform at least that well, or better, to win another term.

An early-August poll from the Los Angeles Times showed Becerra with 55 percent of the vote, compared with 37 percent for Hilton.

Pennsylvania might give Democrats their best bet for down-ballot help, as Shapiro first won in 2022 by 15 percentage points over a far-right legislator who had little money.

Heading into this year, Republicans found early hope when the state treasurer, Garrity, who received more votes in Pennsylvania in 2024 than anyone but Trump, entered the race against Shapiro, but Garrity’s campaign has struggled to launch.

The Cook report summarized the race by noting “a gargantuan cash-on-hand advantage and a decisive polling lead”for the incumbent Democrat.

There’s some hope for ticket-splitting voters, based on findings in the so-called crosstabs of the Inquirer poll showing Shapiro so far ahead. When voters in Northeast Pennsylvania were asked if they preferred a generic Republican or Democrat in Congress, the Republican held a 7-point edge.

That’s some solace for Republican Reps. Rob Bresnahan and Ryan Mackenzie, both of whom narrowly won two years ago on Trump’s coattails in that region of the state.

Take Trump off the ballot, and Democrats believe turnout will doom those Republicans. They believe that will also happen in the Harrisburg area, where a staunch conservative, Rep. Scott Perry, has never modified his stances as his increasingly suburban district has drifted toward the political center.

The most intriguing Pennsylvania race might be just north of Philadelphia, where Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick and his late brother, Mike, have won nine of the last 11 races in that perennial battleground district.

In 2022, when Shapiro won Fitzpatrick’s district by 20 points, the incumbent faced a neophyte Democratic challenger who wasn’t from Bucks County. He won easily, as he did again in 2024 against the same Democrat.

Now, Trump is in the White House and suburban voters are just as angry. The Democratic nominee, Bob Harvie, was born and raised in the county, served as a teacher there, got involved in local politics and was elected to a countywide, three-person commission.

By late June, far earlier than in most races, Fitzpatrick’s campaign unloaded with deeply negative ads about Harvie, a sign of how serious the race had already become.

In late July, appearing with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Shapiro turned a campaign event into a pep rally for the four downballot candidates he hopes will ride into office with him.

“I believe those four races hold the key to who is in the majority in the Congress,” he said.
entries.author: Paul Kane

entries.title: Election Deniers Could Soon Control Elections in Three Swing States
entries.summary: Secretary of state candidates in Nevada, Arizona and Wisconsin have cast doubt on the outcome of the 2020 election.
entries.content:
Candidates with a history of denying the 2020 election results are on the ballot in states across the country this fall, running for the position of secretary of state. If they win, they would be uniquely positioned to exert control over their states’ elections.

At least three presidential battlegrounds — Nevada, Arizona and Wisconsin — are among the states with candidates running in November who have cast doubt on the outcome of the 2020 election. If they win, these candidates could be key allies to President Donald Trump’s efforts to obtain voter rolls and federalize election administration.

“They may just willingly give up election materials. They may just willingly give up cast ballots. They may just willingly give up election machines,” said Edward Caspar, chief counsel for the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, a nonpartisan legal advocacy group. “By having conspiracy-theory-minded individuals in power, it really puts that at risk.”

Unlike in other primaries, the president has rarely weighed in on secretary of state races.

But Alexander Kolodin, the Republican nominee for the position in Arizona, was endorsed by Trump in July. That endorsement could play a key role in November, as it has in several Republican primaries.

“Being a Trump ally, getting the Trump endorsement, and at least supporting Trump's claims of election fraud in 2020, or even beyond that, seem to give candidates an electoral boost,” said Rich Barton, a research fellow for Unite America, a nonpartisan election-reform group. “Over the last few years, election denialism has become something of a litmus test within the Republican Party.”

When asked if the president is looking at these nominees as potential allies in implementing voting restrictions, the White House demurred.

“President Trump wants every state in America to clean up their voter rolls and fully secure their elections, regardless of whether they are led by Democrats or Republicans,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told NOTUS in a statement.

In Nevada, Jim Marchant, who is best known for standing alongside a group of Republicans who signed fake electoral certificates claiming Trump won the 2020 election in Nevada, won his primary in June. He has repeatedly undermined the results of the 2020 election, including in an interview with NBC News in 2022 in which he said, “it’s almost statistically impossible that Joe Biden won.”

It’s Marchant’s second run for secretary of state and his second time facing Cisco Aguilar, the incumbent. Marchant made his first run for the position as the president of the America First Secretary of State Coalition, a group of election deniers who ran for top election roles in 2022. His campaign site this year states that he wants voters to submit proof of citizenship to register and cast ballots, wants results to be hand-counted, and wants universal mail-in voting to end. It also claims that Marchant was “a victim of election fraud” in 2020 when he unsuccessfully ran for Congress.

Marchant’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Next door in Arizona, Kolodin, who helped file a lawsuit that questioned the results of the 2020 election and was later thrown out by a federal judge, won his primary in July. He’s campaigning to “harden systems” and “count every legal vote,” according to his campaign site, against incumbent Secretary of State Adrian Fontes. Kolodin, currently a state representative, pushed and is campaigning on a proposition on track to appear on Arizona ballots this fall that could complicate voting, including through a measure that would require a photo ID to cast an absentee ballot.

“Arizona is a major swing state,” Kolodin said during a PBS debate in May. “The road to the White House runs directly through the Arizona secretary of state's office. It's incumbent that we put somebody in there who's ready to hit the ground Day 1.”

Kolodin’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment.

Wisconsin’s Republican candidate, Jay Schroeder, is running on dismantling the bipartisan Wisconsin Elections Commission, a group of appointees who administer elections statewide. He told NBC in 2022 that he would not have certified the 2020 election results if he were secretary of state. Schroeder, whose campaign also did not respond to a request for comment, refers to the commission as a “failed experiment” on his campaign website.

“The current system is an arbitrary disaster that lacks the transparency Wisconsinites deserve,” Schroeder adds on his site.

One of Trump’s priorities is to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to vote in federal elections and tighten the requirements to vote by mail. The president’s long history of casting doubt on the integrity of elections has weakened voters' trust in election results across party lines.

“They are willing to say things to please the Republican base, to please Donald Trump, even if it's not a credible claim to start with,” said Rick Hasen, an election law expert and law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, of Republican candidates who agree with the president’s claims about the 2020 election. “It suggests that some of these people might be willing to help Trump subvert the outcome of elections if that's what Trump was trying to do.”
entries.author: Adora Brown

entries.title: D.C. Won't Say How It's Using Its Flock Cameras
entries.summary: MPD has the powerful license-plate readers at its disposal, but hasn’t disclosed who has used the data — and for what purpose.
entries.content:
In recent months, Francisco Gómez says that he’s become aware of an eye in the sky that has the power to keep tabs on him when he drives to and from his home in Ward 5.

“They’re hidden in plain sight,” he says, referring to the easy-to-miss cameras that occupy a vantage point some 20 feet above the ground on many light poles across D.C. “When people are moving through their lives in a normal fashion, there’s no avoiding these cameras.”

It’s true that Gómez, and everyone else driving in D.C., is being watched and tracked by the Metropolitan Police Department’s 67 Flock automated license-plate readers. The cameras scan an average of 400,000 tags on a daily basis, storing tag numbers and other identifying characteristics of passing vehicles in a police database for up to three months — longer than many jurisdictions that also use the technology.

Whether that’s a positive thing depends on who you ask.

D.C. police officials say the cameras are a critical investigative tool that have helped solve crimes, including a pair of homicides in 2025, and that they have safeguards in place to limit access to the data collected. Additionally, they point out that D.C. has used some variety of license-plate reader for at least 15 years, without much public concern or controversy.

But critics like Gómez — who recently helped found DeFlock DC, which is demanding that the city’s Metropolitan Police Department pull down the cameras — say Flock technology is significantly more powerful than similar technology used in the past, creating a “vehicle fingerprint” that allows officers to track cars in real time and search for tag numbers across state lines.

That has raised fears about how police could use the cameras. There’s been plenty of recent reporting on cases of abuse in other jurisdictions, where officers have misused the technology to spy on their ex-girlfriends or to track a woman suspected of self-administering an abortion.

It’s not clear whether any such abuse has happened with the District’s Flock license-plate readers, which have been in use since early 2025. That’s in part because MPD has never released any information on how its trove of Flock-generated tag data has been used, and it denied an open records request from NOTUS for the data.

At the start of 2026, after inquiries by D.C. Council member Christina Henderson (I-At Large), MPD stopped allowing other police departments to access its license-plate reader data directly. It now requires them to specifically request data from D.C., part of an effort to ensure the city’s information is used for legitimate criminal investigations. MPD also instituted a new license-plate reader policy in April that requires an annual audit of the data for possible policy violations.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

But for the entire year prior, MPD had allowed thousands of officers across the country nearly unfettered access to its database. And to this day, the department has declined to detail who has used the city’s data — and why.

“My feelings on this have evolved,” Henderson tells NOTUS. “In those initial conversations I had with MPD it definitely seemed like Flock had been rolled out without many guardrails or protocols to ensure that the technology was being used appropriately. But I do think over time MPD has made changes that certainly make me feel more comfortable than in other jurisdictions where they don't have anything in place at all.”

For Gómez, though, no amount of protection will make a difference. To him, the Flock cameras are just one more part in a growing system of surveillance.

“There’s a real chilling effect that happens when you’re monitored at all times,” he said. “Tracking people used to require a warrant and have checks and balances of a judge, but once that wall breaks down you see erosion of free speech and free association and freedom of religion. All of that is extremely concerning.”

Flock Safety did not return a request for comment on the growing backlash to its products. In an automatic reply to an email from NOTUS, the media team wrote that its staff was “currently touching grass and taking a break.”

“Unlike our cameras, we can’t work 24/7, so we’ll get back to you when we’ve had a snack and regained the ability to form coherent sentences,” the email said.

A powerful tool to fight crime

Georgia-based Flock Safety was founded less than a decade ago with the intention of using technology to better help jurisdictions fight crime. It’s now one of the biggest players in the space, valued at more than $8 billion and used in some 6,000 communities across 49 states. More than 100,000 of its signature solar-powered license-plate readers are in use throughout the country.

In D.C., the Metropolitan Police Department signed a $336,000 one-year contract for 67 Flock cameras in December 2024; the contract was later extended through the end of 2026 for another $201,000. (The federal government operates its own Flock cameras on federal land around the city.)
DSC05382 (1).JPG (3504x2336, AR: 1.50)When a car drives past a Flock camera, the technology captures its license plate and other identifying information about it. Because every vehicle is scanned, law enforcement can later query the Flock database to determine when a car was in a certain place.

The tech has proved useful for the District: In May 2025, D.C. officers were able to use MPD’s network of Flock cameras to track and eventually stop three D.C. teenagers who had escaped from a juvenile facility in Pennsylvania and returned to the city in a stolen car, which was then used in a nonfatal shooting. Later in the year, license-plate readers were used to make an arrest in the fatal shooting of Eric Tarpinian-Jachym, a congressional intern working in D.C.

“The expansion of the District’s LPR network has directly contributed to significant public safety gains, helping our investigators identify vehicles connected to serious crimes and locate individuals with outstanding warrants,” said an MPD spokesman, who declined to be identified by his name, in an email.

Because many police departments across the country have adopted the cameras, and because Flock makes it easy for jurisdictions to share information with each other, the cameras have also helped police track suspects across state lines — making it a much more powerful tool for D.C. police than past license-plate reader technology.

“The importance of a shared regional LPR network for the District cannot be overstated,” Jeffery Carroll, MPD’s interim chief, wrote in a February letter to Henderson.

Flock also touts the crimes it says the license-plate readers have helped solve; the company’s website says that more than 10,000 missing people have been located nationally since 2025, and 42% of its customers were able to recover more than half of the stolen vehicles in their respective jurisdictions. Charles Fain Lehman, a scholar at the conservative Manhattan Institute, has created a website called the Flock Crime Prevention Tracker that aggregates news coverage of where Flock has been used to solve crimes.

‘It’s a database of your life’

But critics of the technology say it can be easily abused or used for purposes far afield of local police departments’ stated missions.

The Washington Post recently reported on dozens of cases in which officers used Flock data improperly, including to spy on or stalk wives, girlfriends, exes or romantic prospects. After the Post’s story came out, Flock changed its policies to boost oversight of police officers’ use of its databases and to impose stricter limits on how long it would keep data from scanned tags. (The default was reduced to seven days from 30, though individual jurisdictions can opt to set their own.)
DC: Flock Cameras Under Fire Over Mass Surveilance Concerns (4500x3000, AR: 1.50)
In other cases, local law enforcement has used the Flock lookup tool to aid federal immigration authorities, according to reports from 404 Media and others. For a time, U.S. Customs and Border Protection had direct access to the lookup system through a program that Flock has since paused.

The MPD spokesperson declined to answer questions from NOTUS about whether D.C.’s Flock data had ever been used by federal immigration enforcement, which ramped up in 2025, after President Donald Trump declared a crime emergency in the city and deployed the National Guard.

The department also has not responded to public records requests asking for Flock audit logs, which show who has searched the city’s license-plate data and why. A NOTUS reporter’s January request for that data has gone unanswered for months, in violation of a D.C. law requiring that city agencies turn over documents within 15 business days or cite legal reasons why they won’t.

“I am supremely curious what happened in 2025, especially given what was happening with regard to the federal surges that were taking place here in D.C.,” says Henderson. “Hopefully MPD will be able to be a little more forthright about what happened and what changes took place.”

Nationally, activists and community members are pushing back on Flock. There have been efforts to map the locations of more than 135,000 license-plate readers nationwide (largely from Flock), and an app exists to help drivers find routes that avoid Flock cameras. Activists and journalists have pushed to acquire logs of Flock database searches through open-records requests, which have since been used to create an online tool that people can use to check if their license plate has been scanned by a Flock camera.

Locally, some residents in Virginia have started fighting the use of the technology, including in Alexandria, Prince William County and Fairfax County.

“This gets sold as a crime database. It is not. It’s a database of you living your life. It is your movements, your patterns when you’re living your life. That’s government overreach,” said Steven Keener, the director of the Center for Crime, Equity and Justice Research and Policy at Christopher Newport University, during an anti-Flock event in Fairfax County last weekend.

In D.C., members of the DeFlock DC group have opted for more low-tech tactics to raise awareness: Over the summer they put signs reading, “Smile! You’re being spied on,” on every light pole with a Flock camera on it. In mid-August, the group hosted its first public meeting at the MLK Memorial Library; more than three-dozen people attended.

Even some advocates of using Flock concede that some of the worries about its power and possible abuse can’t be ignored. This week, the International Association of Chiefs of Police issued a statement hailing the technology’s potential for fighting crime, while recognizing the need for “strong safeguards” to protect individual rights and maintain public confidence.

‘We have to figure out what the balance is’

In January, in his first month as interim chief, Carroll directed MPD to cease participation in Flock’s National Lookup Tool, which had previously allowed participating departments across the country to search the city’s data.
National Guard Shooting (6000x4000, AR: 1.50)Now, MPD requires other police agencies to enter into a memorandum of agreement before receiving access to D.C.’s Flock data. Such agreements require compliance with D.C. laws, including a local law that prohibits the city from aiding interstate investigations into abortions, Carroll wrote in his letter to Henderson. D.C. also grants other requests for information from its cameras, including requests from federal agencies, on a case-by-case basis, provided there’s a legitimate law enforcement purpose, Carroll said.

In April, MPD also began requiring yearly audits of the data to ensure the rules were being followed. Henderson says lawmakers should continue exploring these types of limits on the technology, while recognizing that license-plate readers can be helpful for improving public safety.

“I think we have to figure out what the balance is, and I think that’s the conversation that we should be having as policymakers,” she says.

But despite the policy updates, some information about the city’s Flock use remains elusive. Asked whether the department had initiated an audit of the data and whether it would commit to publicly releasing the Flock audit log records, the MPD spokesperson declined to answer.

“At this time, we have provided all the information we have available on this matter,” he wrote in an email on Monday.
